layers.title: The Root
layers.subtitle: From Rahima — a mercy that is vast, encompassing, and a permanent divine attribute.
layers.source: Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, The Ninety-Nine Names of Allah (memorisation tool with meanings)
layers.content:
The name Ar-Rahman comes from the Arabic root ra-ha-ma (ر-ح-م), which carries the meaning of a vast, encompassing, tender mercy — a mercy so extensive it covers everything in creation.

The scholars distinguish between two forms:

Ar-Rahman (الرَّحْمَٰنُ) — on the pattern fa'lan (فَعْلَان), which indicates fullness, intensity, and permanence. It refers to the attribute of mercy itself as it exists in Allah's own being — vast and comprehensive beyond anything creation can contain.

Ar-Raheem (الرَّحِيمُ) — on the pattern fa'eel (فَعِيل), which indicates the action of that mercy being directed outward toward creation.

Shikh Ibn Uthaymeen clarifies this distinction: "Ar-Rahman is with regards to Allah's self — that He has Himself extreme mercy. Ar-Raheem is that of His bestowing mercy upon the creation with regards to His action."

In other words: Ar-Rahman describes what Allah IS. Ar-Raheem describes what Allah DOES. The first is the ocean; the second is the rain that falls from it.

Ar-Rahman appears as a proper name — unique to Allah. No human being can be called Ar-Rahman. This distinguishes it from other names like Raheem or Kareem, which can be attributes of people. Ar-Rahman belongs to Allah alone.

layers.title: The Meaning
layers.subtitle: A mercy so vast it covers even those who rebel against its source.
layers.source: Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, The Ninety-Nine Names of Allah
layers.content:
Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen defines Ar-Rahman as: "The merciful one who has as His attribute mercy, the one possessing tremendous and extensive mercy."

The theological depth of this name is staggering. Allah's mercy as Ar-Rahman covers all of creation without exception — believer and disbeliever, the obedient and the disobedient, the human and the animal, the seen and the unseen. The rain falls on the field of the one who prays and the one who does not. The oxygen sustains the lungs of the believer and the lungs of the one who denies the Giver of breath.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has one hundred mercies. He sent down one of them among the jinn, humans, animals, and insects — by it they show compassion and mercy to one another. By it, the wild animal shows compassion to her young. Allah has retained ninety-nine mercies with which He will show mercy to His servants on the Day of Resurrection." (Sahih Muslim).

This means: everything we experience of mercy in this world — the mother's love for her child, the friend who stays when it is hard to stay, the kindness of a stranger — is a single drop from a mercy of one hundred parts. And ninety-nine of those parts have not yet been revealed.

The name Ar-Rahman opens Surah Al-Fatiha — the prayer Muslims say seventeen times a day minimum. Before we ask for anything, before we describe the Day of Judgment, before we ask for guidance — we begin with: In the name of Allah, the Extremely Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy. Mercy is the first quality of Allah declared in the Book.

layers.title: In the Quran
layers.subtitle: 57 times, Ar-Rahman appears in the Quran — including an entire surah in its name.
layers.source: Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, The Ninety-Nine Names of Allah; Quran direct
layers.content:
Ar-Rahman appears 57 times in the Quran — as an attribute, as a name, and as the title of an entire surah. Surah Ar-Rahman (Chapter 55) is one of the most celebrated chapters of the Quran, structured around the repeated question: "Which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?" (Quran 55:13).

The surah opens: "Ar-Rahman — He taught the Quran. He created man. He taught him eloquence." (Quran 55:1-4). Notice the order: the first act of the Extremely Merciful is not creation — it is teaching. Before man is mentioned, the Quran is mentioned. The greatest mercy is revelation — being shown the truth.

In Surah Maryam, when Maryam saw Jibreel for the first time and was frightened, she said: "I seek refuge with the Extremely Merciful from you." (Quran 19:18). She turned to Ar-Rahman at the moment of fear — not to Al-Jabbar (the Compeller) or Al-Qawi (the Strong), but to the Extremely Merciful. This is how the companions and prophets turned to Allah in fear: to His mercy, not His power.

In Surah Ta-Ha, the Throne of Allah is described: "The Extremely Merciful has risen over the Throne." (Quran 20:5). Sovereignty and mercy are united at the highest point. The one who rules all creation rules with mercy at the very centre of His governance.

The name Ar-Rahman appears frequently alongside Ar-Raheem — the pairing opening every surah of the Quran except At-Tawbah. This pairing is the most repeated phrase in the Book of Allah — approximately 114 times across the full text.

layers.title: The Scholar
layers.subtitle: Ibnul-Qayyim: Ar-Rahman is the name that contains all other names.
layers.source: Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, The Ninety-Nine Names of Allah, citing Ibnul-Qayyim
layers.content:
The scholars gave Ar-Rahman a position unlike any other divine attribute. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen records the teaching of Ibnul-Qayyim on the name Allah itself, which applies also to Ar-Rahman — that it is a name of comprehensiveness. To know Ar-Rahman is to understand the lens through which all other names are seen.

The Quran instructs: "Call upon Allah or call upon Ar-Rahman — by whichever you call, for to Him belong the most beautiful names." (Quran 17:110). This verse places Ar-Rahman directly alongside the proper name Allah — indicating its supreme rank among the names.

Shikh Ibn Uthaymeen writes of the name Allah in his recorded commentary: "The name Allah indicates all of the perfect names and lofty attributes in all three ways of indication since it indicates His divinity, which indicates affirmation of all the characteristics of divinity for Him." The scholars hold the same for Ar-Rahman — it is a comprehensive name that encompasses every expression of divine goodness.

The classical scholars further noted: Ar-Rahman cannot be taken as a name by any created being. When the people of Yamama gave the false prophet Musaylimah the title Al-Rahman, this was among the gravest of his crimes — appropriating a divine name exclusively belonging to Allah.

Ibnul-Qayyim taught that whenever a servant calls upon Allah using one of the beautiful names, they are not only asking for help — they are affirming something about the nature of the One they are calling. Calling upon Ar-Rahman is an act of certainty: I believe Your mercy is real, extensive, and that it covers even me, even now.

layers.title: Your Reflection
layers.subtitle: How does knowing Allah is Ar-Rahman change what you believe about yourself?
layers.source: Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, The Ninety-Nine Names of Allah
layers.content:
"Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves — do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful." (Quran 39:53)

This is perhaps the most expansive promise in the Quran — and it is addressed to those who have "transgressed against themselves." Not to the righteous. Not to those who have earned it. To those who have failed.

Ar-Rahman is the name that makes repentance possible. If Allah's mercy were limited — if it could run out, if it could be exhausted by enough failure — then there would be a point beyond which return was impossible. But Ar-Rahman describes a mercy that is an eternal divine attribute. It does not diminish. It does not expire.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah is more merciful to His servant than a mother is to her child." A mother's mercy — which is among the most powerful forces in human experience — is itself derived from Ar-Rahman. The source of all mercy is infinitely greater than its greatest expression in creation.

Shikh Ibn Uthaymeen's text is presented as a memorisation tool — not for information alone, but for dhikr. To say Ar-Rahman in salah, in du'a, in moments of fear or failure, is to activate this knowledge. The name is not merely a description. It is an address.

Reflect: Is there something you believe Allah cannot forgive you for? If yes — that belief contradicts this name. The name Ar-Rahman, correctly understood, makes despair about one's own soul theologically unjustifiable. Not because the sin does not matter — but because the mercy is greater.

quiz.prompt: According to Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, what is the key grammatical difference between Ar-Rahman and Ar-Raheem, and what does it indicate?

options.text: Ar-Rahman is masculine and Ar-Raheem is the general form — no theological difference
Ar-Rahman (fa'lan pattern) indicates the attribute of mercy in Allah's own being; Ar-Raheem (fa'eel pattern) indicates mercy directed in action toward creation
Ar-Rahman is used only for the dunya; Ar-Raheem is used only for the akhirah
Ar-Rahman means forgiveness; Ar-Raheem means compassion — they refer to separate qualities

quiz.citation: Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, The Ninety-Nine Names of Allah — note on Ar-Rahman and Ar-Raheem
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Uthaymeen writes: 'Ar-Rahman is with regards to Allah's self — that He has Himself extreme mercy. Ar-Raheem is that of His bestowing mercy upon the creation with regards to His action.' The first describes what Allah IS; the second describes what Allah DOES. Understanding this distinction deepens how we call upon these names in du'a.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ said Allah has one hundred mercies. How many did He send to the world, and what did He retain?

options.text: Fifty mercies sent; fifty retained for the Day of Resurrection
Ten mercies sent; ninety retained
One mercy sent; ninety-nine retained for the Day of Resurrection
All one hundred were sent, spread across all creation

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim — narration on the one hundred mercies
quiz.scholar_reflection: By this one mercy — a single drop from one hundred — mothers love their children, creatures show compassion to each other, and every act of kindness in this world exists. Ninety-nine parts remain unrevealed, reserved for the Day of Resurrection. This is the scale of Ar-Rahman.

quiz.prompt: In Surah Ar-Rahman (Chapter 55), what is the first act attributed to Ar-Rahman — before the creation of man is mentioned?

options.text: He created the heavens and the earth
He sent down rain and provisions
He taught the Quran
He made a covenant with every soul

quiz.citation: Quran 55:1-4 — 'Ar-Rahman — He taught the Quran. He created man. He taught him eloquence.'
quiz.scholar_reflection: Before creation is mentioned, revelation is mentioned. The Quran precedes man in the surah of Ar-Rahman. This is the scholars' evidence that the greatest mercy of Allah toward humanity is not sustenance, health, or even life — it is guidance. To be shown truth is the highest mercy.

quiz.prompt: In Surah Maryam, when Maryam was frightened upon seeing Jibreel, which name of Allah did she invoke for protection?

options.text: Al-Jabbar — the Compeller
Al-Hafeedh — the Guardian
Ar-Rahman — the Extremely Merciful
Al-Mu'min — the Granter of Security

quiz.citation: Quran 19:18 — Maryam says: 'I seek refuge with the Extremely Merciful from you'
quiz.scholar_reflection: In a moment of fear, Maryam turned to Ar-Rahman — not to the name of power or protection, but to mercy. This teaches us that when frightened, when vulnerable, when overwhelmed — the most natural place to turn is to the mercy of Allah. Ar-Rahman is not only the name of comfort; it is the name that makes us feel safe to turn.

quiz.prompt: Why is Ar-Rahman considered unique among the beautiful names in a way that Raheem, Kareem, or Haleem are not?

options.text: It appears more times in the Quran than any other name
It can only be used as a name for Allah — no human being can be called Ar-Rahman
It is the only name used in du'a — other names are only for praise
It is the only name that directly causes rain and mercy to descend

quiz.citation: Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, The Ninety-Nine Names of Allah — on the exclusivity of Ar-Rahman
quiz.scholar_reflection: Names like Raheem, Kareem, Haleem can all be attributes of human beings — a man can be merciful, generous, or forbearing. But Ar-Rahman is reserved exclusively for Allah. When the false prophet Musaylimah was called Al-Rahman, this was among his gravest offences. The name belongs to Allah alone.

quiz.prompt: The Quran says: 'O My servants who have transgressed against themselves — do not despair of the mercy of Allah.' (39:53). Is there something in your own life you have difficulty believing Allah's mercy covers?

options.text: A repeated sin — something I keep returning to despite knowing better
A past action I can't undo, whose consequences still affect others
A period of my life where I was far from Allah and don't feel I deserve His mercy now
I generally trust Allah's mercy — my struggle is more with forgiving myself

quiz.citation: Quran 39:53 — addressed to those who have 'transgressed against themselves'
quiz.scholar_reflection: This ayah was addressed specifically to those who have sinned — not to the righteous. The scholars note it is one of the most expansive verses on tawbah in the Quran. 'Indeed, Allah forgives all sins' — this is not a general statement. It is a direct promise to the specific person reading it. Ar-Rahman's mercy is not limited by the size of the failure.
quiz.slider_label: How fully do I believe Allah's mercy covers the darkest parts of my own past? (Very little → Completely)

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ said Allah is more merciful to His servant than a mother is to her child. Think of the most loving relationship in your life. Which of these best describes how you relate to the idea that Allah's mercy exceeds even that?

options.text: I believe it intellectually but struggle to feel it — my experience of Allah feels more distant
It reshapes how I make du'a — I approach Allah with expectation, not just hope
It challenges my image of Allah as primarily strict or demanding
It gives me permission to ask for things I previously thought were too small or selfish to ask for

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — 'Allah is more merciful to His servant than a mother is to her child'
quiz.scholar_reflection: The scholars use this hadith to establish that the default relationship between Allah and His servants is mercy — not severity. Severity is real, but it comes after persistent rejection of mercy. A mother who loves her child with every fibre of her being is giving her child a drop of the mercy that belongs to Ar-Rahman.
quiz.slider_label: How much do I feel Allah's mercy in my daily life, not just believe it? (Rarely → Constantly)

quiz.prompt: Ar-Rahman opens every Surah (except At-Tawbah) through Bismillah. This means every time Muslims begin a significant action with Bismillah, they invoke this name. Which of these most reflects how you experience the act of saying Bismillah?

options.text: Mostly habit — I say it but rarely pause to feel its meaning
A genuine sense of seeking help and placing the action under Allah's mercy
A reminder that what I am about to do should be something I'm not ashamed for Allah to witness
I forget it often — and feel more conscious of Allah's presence when I remember to say it

quiz.citation: Bismillahir-Rahmanir-Raheem — opening of 113 surahs of the Quran
quiz.scholar_reflection: The scholars taught that Bismillah is not merely an opening formula — it is an act of seeking blessing (barakah) and of placing one's action under the name of Allah. To say Bismillahir-Rahmanir-Raheem is to declare: what I am about to do, I do in the name of the One whose mercy is my hope.
quiz.slider_label: How consciously do I invoke Allah's mercy through Bismillah? (Automatically/unconsciously → Deliberately and with presence)

quiz.prompt: Ninety-nine parts of Allah's mercy are reserved for the Day of Resurrection. When you imagine standing before Allah on that Day, which of these best describes what you feel?

options.text: Fear — I am afraid of my account and what I have not done
Hope — I believe Ar-Rahman's mercy will outweigh my failures
Both, shifting — fear when I think of my sins, hope when I remember this name
Distance — the Day of Judgment feels abstract and far away to me

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim — one hundred mercies, ninety-nine reserved for Yawm al-Qiyamah
quiz.scholar_reflection: The scholars held that a Muslim should stand between fear and hope — al-khawf and ar-raja. Too much fear without hope leads to despair, which is itself forbidden. Too much hope without fear leads to negligence. The knowledge that ninety-nine parts of mercy remain for the Day of Resurrection is meant to produce hope in the heart — not complacency.
quiz.slider_label: In my relationship with Allah, how balanced am I between fear and hope? (Overwhelmingly fear → Overwhelmingly hope)

quiz.prompt: Ar-Rahman's mercy covers all of creation — believer and disbeliever, human and animal, those who pray and those who do not. How does knowing this affect how you see people who have turned away from Allah?

options.text: It makes me more patient — if Allah still sustains them, who am I to write them off
It is difficult — I understand it but feel tension between mercy and justice
It makes me want to be a vehicle of that mercy — to show people what they are rejecting
It humbles me — I remember how many times Allah sustained me even when I was distant from Him

quiz.citation: Quran 55:13 — 'Which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?'
quiz.scholar_reflection: The general mercy of Ar-Rahman covers all of creation. This does not mean all are equal before Allah — it means that Allah's mercy in sustaining, providing, and caring for His creation extends to everyone. Understanding this should soften how we see people who are not yet where we hope they will be — and remind us that we too were once in different places.
quiz.slider_label: How much does knowing Allah's mercy is universal affect my compassion toward people who are distant from Him? (Very little → Significantly)
